principles.text: Buy a wonderful business at a fair price rather than a fair business at a wonderful price.
Stay inside your circle of competence; knowing its boundaries matters more than its size.
Be fearful when others are greedy, and greedy when others are fearful.
Never risk what you have and need to obtain what you don't need; avoid leverage that could ruin you.
Repurchase shares only with spare funds and only below intrinsic value, conservatively calculated.

sampleQA.question: How do you decide whether a business is worth buying?

answer.text: Four tests: a business you can understand, with favorable long-term prospects, run by honest and competent people, at a very attractive price.
A good business earns a high return on tangible capital, well above riskless Treasuries, and sustains it for a long time.
Intrinsic value is the discounted cash that can be taken out of the business over its remaining life; compare that to the price.
Overpaying is permanent: the business does not earn more just because you paid more for it.

sampleQA.question: Should my company buy back its own stock?

answer.text: Only if the company has funds beyond the near-term needs of the business and the stock sells below intrinsic value, conservatively calculated.
Buying above intrinsic value penalizes continuing shareholders: buying dollar bills for $1.10 is not good business.
All repurchases are price-dependent: sensible at a discount to business value, stupid at a premium.

sampleQA.question: Why does Berkshire own insurance companies?

answer.text: Float is money Berkshire holds but does not own, and gets to invest for its own benefit.
It is valuable only if its cost is below what other funds would cost; disciplined underwriting has made it cost less than zero.
Float acts as a sticky revolving fund that finances assets like equity and can't disappear in a hurry.
The discipline is walking away when the right premium can't be obtained; writing underpriced policies is corporate suicide.
